Aboard his KTM 300 EXC, the German controlled the race from the opening Off-Road Stage to the finish, eventually sealing the overall win in Romania by more than an hour. KTM’s Manuel Lettenbichler climbs to the top of this hill en route to his seventh career victory at the Red Bull Romaniacs Hard Enduro Rally in Romania. He joins Graham Jarvis as a seven-time winner of the race. Second overall went to Sherco’s Teodor Kabakchiev, with Beta’s James Moore, KTM rider Matthew Green and GasGas’ Mitch Brightmore. The top American finisher was KTM rider Tobin Miller in 16th overall. The week began with the Prologue in Sibiu’s spectacular city center, where Lettenbichler topped qualifying before finishing third in the multi-lap final. “Mani” then hit the mountain stages in style, winning Off-Road day one by almost eight minutes to move into the overall lead. Another commanding victory on Off-Road day two extended the German’s advantage to over 19 minutes. Despite narrowly missing out on the Off-Road day three win by less than one minute after an intense battle with the Bulgarian, Kabakchiev, Mani comfortably retained his race lead heading into the final day. Lettenbichler recorded his seventh victory at the Red Bull Romaniacs Hard Enduro. Lettenbichler sealed the victory on Off-Road day four, dominating the final stage by 44 minutes over Kabakchiev. The result secured the overall win by one hour and three minutes, completing one of the most commanding performances in Red Bull Romaniacs history. The triumph marks Mani’s seventh career victory at the event, equaling the all-time record with Graham Jarvis, while also extending his remarkable run to four consecutive Red Bull Romaniacs wins. Lettenbichler (1) battles Kabakchiev (11) during the prologue. “It’s honestly hard to put into words,” Lettenbichler said. “Riding through the final grass fields, I was just thinking about how far my career has come. To win Red Bull Romaniacs for the seventh time is something I never expected, and it’s an unreal feeling. Every victory here takes so much hard work and preparation, so this one is special. I enjoyed the riding this week. There were some incredibly tough sections, but I was able to ride my own race, especially on the final day, and really enjoy it. Crossing the finish line is always an amazing feeling, and one of the best parts of Romaniacs is sharing the experience with so many riders from all over the world. Everyone goes through the same challenges out there, and that makes this event really unique.” CN This year’s podium was made up of Lettenbichler (center), Sherco’s Teodor Kabakchiev (left) and Beta’s James Moore. 2026 Red Bull Romaniacs Results OVERALL (Top 10) Manuel Lettenbichler (KTM) 22:14:41 Teodor Kabakchiev (She) +1:03:27 James Moore (Bet) +2:20:22 Matthew Green (KTM) +2:50:18 Mitch Brightmore (GG) +2:53:17 Michael Walkner (GG) +3:36:44 Lorenzo Gandola (She) +4:25:59 Thomas Scales (Bet) +5:46:45 Sonny Goggia (KTM) +6:5:44 David Cyprian (KTM) +6:28:14 READ MORE Motorcycle Racing Hub → READ MORE Hard Enduro → Cycle News Magazine Top Stories 2026 Unadilla Pro Motocross Results (Updated) 2026 MotoAmerica VIR Results (Updated) 2026 Washougal Pro Motocross Results (Updated) Six American World Champions Reunite at Laguna Seca for Historic Celebration of Japanese Motorsport Zach Osborne Returns To Pro Motocross Latest Videos Press Releases view all > Lucas Coenen to Miss Swedish MXGP to Continue Hip Recovery Norton Motorcycles Gives Insight Into Manx R Research & Development Program Ducati North America to Support AMA Motorcycle Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony as Livestream Sponsor Yamaha Motor Corporation Joins as Presenting Sponsor of AMA Motorcycle Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony No Wimps 2027 Registration Now Open AIMExpo Introduces The Builders Cup Pro Motocross Previews 2026 Unadilla National Project Enduro for Vets Partners with 2026 Red Bull Tennessee Knockout 2026 Industry Speedway Results

Composite: AFP via Getty Images, CNP/Shutterstock Maha's Gold Standard Trump administration Medical researcher who touted Covid ‘cure’ and was hailed by Dr Oz under fire over ethics New findings further call into question scientific judgment of current health leaders in the Trump administration Michelle R Smith Wed 19 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 08.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A French researcher whose work was praised by Donald Trump and Dr Mehmet Oz during the Covid-19 pandemic published hundreds of papers with “substantial” ethical and legal concerns, according to a new analysis. An international team of scientists found concerns in 853 articles published by the Institut Hospitalo-Universitaire Méditerranée Infection, or the IHU, hundreds more than previously flagged by past investigations into work at the large research hospital. Of those, institute founder Didier Raoult was listed as co-author on 758 of them, according to one of the researchers behind the new analysis. Raoult rocketed to the global stage in March 2020, when the novel virus was spreading unchecked and killing people across the world. He and several colleagues published research that claimed hydroxychloroquine – a drug used for malaria and certain autoimmune conditions – was found to be an effective treatment for Covid-19, especially in combination with the drug azithromycin. RFK Jr under fire for ‘bullying’ letter to scientific journal Read more Trump at the time called Raoult’s research on hydroxychloroquine a “gamechanger”, though many scientists disagreed and raised concerns about the quality of the research, including Dr Anthony Fauci , then a top Trump adviser. Despite those calls for caution, Oz, who now heads the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, an agency responsible for $1.6tn in spending, echoed Trump at the time in calling Raoult’s work a gamechanger. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, made a high-profile visit to the institute and met with Raoult. Later, Robert F Kennedy Jr called Raoult’s work “powerful” and dedicated a book he wrote that blasted Fauci in part to Raoult. The drug has not been shown to be effective as a Covid-19 treatment, and the paper was ultimately retracted for ethical and scientific reasons in 2025. But it had become one of the most famous articles of the pandemic era, having been cited thousands of times. The new findings further call into question the scientific judgment of current health leaders in the Trump administration, who have said they are committed to restoring what they call “gold-standard science” informing federal policy. A Republican-led committee of the US Senate recently voted to hold Fauci in contempt for pleading the fifth during a hearing about Covid-19’s origins. View image in fullscreen A screengrab of a video posted to Dr Mehmet Oz’s Facebook page on 23 March 2020, showing him in conversation with Dr Didier Raoult. Photograph: Dr Mehmet Oz via Facebook “If Oz had reviewed/read the study correctly he would have found many of the problems” that were raised about it, said Lonni Besançon, an assistant professor in data visualization at Linköping University in Sweden and a member of the international research team that did the new analysis, which was published this month in the journal Research Integrity and Peer Review. Besançon said the now-retracted article was used to claim there was a cure for Covid, led to shortages of hydroxychloroquine and drove scientists to pour their attention into researching that drug rather than other promising leads. It also fueled conspiracy theories from people who argued the article was being attacked “because if there was a cure for Covid then they couldn’t sell their vaccines”, he said. “A lot of time was wasted,” Besançon said. “It’s been a massively influential paper, and it’s also been used to push for an antivax agenda.” Trump, Oz and Kennedy promoted the research Fauci, who was a leading member of the White House coronavirus taskforce, was asked at a news conference with Trump on 20 March 2020 whether there was evidence hydroxychloroquine could be used to combat Covid-19. Fauci, standing with the president, replied, “The answer is no,” called such research “ anecdotal evidence ” and noted it was not done in a controlled clinical trial. He called for rigorous scientific research to show whether it would be both safe and effective. But the next day, Trump cited Raoult’s research in a tweet, saying hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin “have a real chance to be one of the biggest game changers in the history of medicine” and saying he hoped they would be put in use immediately. Three studies used by RFK Jr and allies to justify controversial vaccine policy changes facing new scrutiny Read more Two days later, Oz, then a TV personality and physician, appeared on Fox & Friends , where he said he was “flabbergasted” by Raoult’s research and urged the US government to procure the drug. “I read the study. I was stunned. Literally, a jaw dropped. I didn’t know it was possible,” Oz said. While Oz noted it had not been a randomized trial and said he was launching his own such trial to replicate Raoult’s findings, he also called the French work a “gamechanger”. “The data is so strong, I completely understand why America wants to start taking these pills,” Oz said, before adding that more data was needed. Publicly, Oz interviewed Raoult multiple times in March and April for his TV show. Behind the scenes, Oz was emailing Trump administration officials to highlight the research, according to emails later obtained by a US House select committee on the coronavirus crisis. In them, Oz vouched for the quality of Raoult’s research. “You should know that the French researcher confirmed clinical benefits but needs more data so will not release report for another 10 days. These findings offer hope to our people,” Oz wrote on 22 March . He called it a “ potential pandemic solution ” in an email to Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Six days later, he wrote that Raoult had sent him updated research and that “the treatment appears safe and results are better than expected”. Trump’s current health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, then leading the anti-vaccine activist group Children’s Health Defense , named Raoult among the “heroic” scientists to whom he dedicated his 2021 book, The Real Anthony Fauci. Kennedy’s book attacked Fauci for his stance toward hydroxychloroquine. The Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not return requests for comment about Kennedy’s and Oz’s promotion of Raoult’s work. Widespread ethical problems The team of researchers has been digging into the IHU’s work for years. They initially looked at 2,674 papers published by the institute between 1994 and 2024 and discovered various ethical concerns in 853 of them. For example, the team noted that French law requires certain steps be taken when using human subjects in biomedical research in order to protect people from harm. The team estimates that at least 78 articles describe biomedical research “that appears not to comply with the applicable French law”, they wrote. The team also found 343 articles in which no ethics approvals were ever recorded, dozens of approvals that appear to have been obtained retrospectively after the study began and repeated reuse of ethics approvals for different studies, among other issues. Trump’s pick for surgeon general sells supplement with ingredient banned by Pentagon Read more They noted that while issues such as fraud and plagiarism often get more attention when it comes to research misconduct, ethical problems can undermine public trust in research and in the scientific process. The findings have in the past few years led to 64 articles being retracted and 270 being tagged with an “ expression of concern ”, which can indicate that major and credible concerns have been raised about the article, the team wrote. They called for additional review of the institute’s work “to ensure that the scientific record is corrected where appropriate”. It was critical of the institute as well as of Aix-Marseille University, which they said was largely responsible for overseeing the work there. “These findings raise broader questions regarding the university’s governance and oversight mechanisms,” they wrote. Besançon said millions of euros in research funds were “thrown out the window” due to the poor research practices at the IHU, and many students were improperly trained in scientific practices. “For me, this is what’s important,” he said in an interview. “To make sure we can push for good, scrutinizable and responsible science.” The university said in a statement that it “conscientiously and responsibly” took “all measures within its remit” from when it was first alerted to problems in 2020. It said it did its own investigation and transferred its findings to relevant authorities, then fully cooperated with the investigations. It said it also “engaged with scientific publishers” and has “continuously strengthened its prevention, support and oversight mechanisms”. “Research ethics and research integrity are fundamental pillars of Aix Marseille University’s research policy and are at the heart of its commitment to responsible, rigorous and high-quality research,” it said. Raoult retired in 2021. Though he responded to emails sent to him by the Guardian, he did not address questions about his research and the team’s analysis. In the past, he has stood by his research and criticized decisions to retract his studies. He told Science magazine in 2024 that he followed ethical regulations. The Guardian also sought comment from the IHU. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/30/soun.text: Animasyros, one of Europe's major animation festivals, recently wrapped up its 19th consecutive year of celebrations in Ermoupoli, flying the flag for the Greece's biggest International Animation Festival.Beyond the seven competition sections (International, Student, K.ID.S, AnimaPride, National Competition, TV & Commissioned Films and Feature Films), this year's edition included a special focus on Irish animation, a theme marking 200 years of Ermoupoli, educational workshops, parallel events, international collaborations and the Market, which has now become a key reference point for the entire industry in the Eastern Mediterranean.Vassilis Karamitssanis, President of the Animasyros International Festival, spoke to Euronews about what the event has achieved so far and what lies ahead next year, when Animasyros celebrates its 20th anniversary:"In the 18-19 years that Animasyros has been in the spotlight, or that have elapsed since its founding back in 2008, I believe it has become the most important hub for animation in the Mediterranean and in Greece. It places strong emphasis on showcasing Greek and European talent around the world and also aims to highlight new techniques and technologies in the field of animation, which I consider to be the key to a sustainable future for the audiovisual sector in general and for European animation in particular."Listen upOne of the most prominent guests at this year's edition was the internationally recognised and multi-award-winning sound designer Olivier Calvert.With a long track record of collaborations with leading directors and organisations, the Montreal-based Canadian creator has shaped the sonic universe of numerous acclaimed productions, including the Oscar-nominated short film The Girl Who Cried Pearls. He was also part of the Oscar-winning sound team for Denis Villeneuve's Arrival.During the festival, Calvert presented a masterclass devoted to sound as a decisive storytelling tool. The festival paid tribute to his work and screened a selection of films:"Sound design shapes the overall sound of a film, which means you can work with its sonic environment. It can be realistic – birds, traffic noise, the sea, the waves. But it can also operate on a subconscious level. You can really create tension in a scene by adding other sounds beneath the music or the voice, or by removing sounds," explained Calvert."You can build tension that way. It is important, because sound is the filter through which you look at the image. It gives you the emotion with which you perceive that image. There is a saying I like very much, which was also the subtitle of my workshop: 'The image is the body, but sound is the soul'.""For me, it is the whole emotional landscape of the film. It is all the sound, not just the music. Every sound is music in a way, so it contributes to the emotional impact of the film. There is a big difference between fiction films and animation. In live-action films you first create sound for a normal environment. In animation everything is constructed, an entirely new world, so why should the sound be natural, real? In an animated film we do not need the sound to be realistic. So yes, we can create a completely different world, a unique world. A new universe to discover, both in terms of image and in terms of sound."Sometimes I get involved very early in the creative process, especially with directors I have already worked with. They now bring me in at a very early stage, because we can shape the film using sound as a storytelling device. You can tell a story purely with images and you can tell a story purely with sounds. So the challenge is to build a story through the collaboration between images and sounds. That is where I can help the director achieve this. I am something like an artistic director for sound," added Calvert."I dare to take on the role of adviser for them. As soon as I am hired for a film, we start to discuss ideas around it. And we work together with the composer. I am not a composer. That is why I always collaborate with someone else on the sound, who is the composer. This trio (director, composer and sound designer) is very important. For me the soundtrack of a film is a whole. There is the music on the one hand and the sound effects on the other. Everything goes together, so it is a major collaboration between director, composer and sound designer. Yes, there is great synergy between the three."Cross-border collaborationsThis year's festival opened with the Greek premiere of Decorado by Goya-winning Spanish creator Alberto Vásquez (Unicorn Wars, Birdboy: The Forgotten Children), with the support of the Embassy of Spain in Greece and the Cervantes Institute. The film, which received the Paul Grimault award at this year's Annecy animation festival, recalls The Truman Show in animated form.It is an existential black comedy about the absurdity of modern life and the control that others seek to impose on us, featuring the director's trademark macabre visual style, which combines innocence and dark humour with a dystopian contemporary reality.José Luis Ágreda, the film's creative director spoke to Euronews about the project: "Decorado, the film we presented here at Animasyros, is a parable, a dark parable about our society and the way in which each of us, every individual, feels within it. The film is also about how society or, more specifically, companies try to dehumanise people."The story is about a man without a job for whom everything seems strange. He does not perceive things as reality because they have nothing to do with him. There is humour and these funny animal characters," said Ágreda. "But when the viewer enters the world of the film, they realise that it is a dystopia, a universe that becomes ever darker. And they understand that it concerns them, as it reflects today's world. This was our way of getting audiences to think about what is happening around us today.""The animation style we use has many references to classic Disney cartoons. I mean classic American animation. But we give it a different twist, so that viewers do not immediately recognise it, while at the same time realising that there is something strange. It is as if we have a very happy world, like the society they try to sell us, but inside it there is something rotten. So we try to work with these characters and this kind of environment, yet we create odd colours, unusual combinations of colours. In the end, people feel: 'OK, this is a nightmare, not a dream'.""What happens to the hero, Arnold, is very similar to what we experience on social media. You feel that you are at the centre of attention and of everything, but you are not. Everything around you is constructed, fake, not real. That is because we live in a society that stays with appearance and not with being. This is the idea behind our film: that we are on a stage, on a set, where we play a role while ignoring what is really happening around us. We do not realise that everything around us is fabricated. This gives us the impression that everything is perfect. The result? We do not deal with the great problems of our society."The AwardsThe Grand Prize of the International Competition at the 19th Animasyros was awarded to Please by Anna Mantzaris, while the prize in the Greek Competition went to Konstantinos Demis for The Dog.In the Student Competition, the award was won by Gauze, a film about Palestine created by a team of five students from GOBELINS Paris, Noran Fikri Alezabi, Nicholas Arujah, Xinyue Ma, Yulin YUE and Xiaonan Zhou.In the Television and Commissioned Films category, the prize went to Saltwater by Eilidh Nicoll from the United Kingdom. The Animapride competition section features films with LGBTQI+ content and showcases creativity, queer expression and acceptance. The jury awarded its prize to Eyeliner by Aisha Boujilouli. The first prize in the K.ID.S category was given to The Eagle and the Kinglet by Paul Jadoul from the Czech Republic.The Audience Award at Animasyros was collected by Martin Lund's Unstoppable, a subversive and emotional, humourous adventure film.
